name: Gustave Flaubert
importanceReason: He pushed authorial commentary out of the sentence and established free indirect discourse as a way of layering a character's consciousness and the narrator's voice within a single sentence. His discipline of rewriting a sentence for days to find the right word moved the novel from improvised storytelling to designed prose, and became the starting point for the 20th-century novel's treatment of point-of-view control as a basic technique. In the unfinished final work Bouvard and Pécuchet, his attempt to collect and catalogue clichés anticipated the 20th-century anti-novel, which takes received opinion itself as its subject.
readingEntryReason: As his signature work with strong narrative drive, it can be read to completion as a single self-contained book, and it is the one entry point where free indirect discourse can be recognized even in translation.
readingWarning: Starting with Salammbô or Bouvard and Pécuchet, with their archaeological detail and catalogues of erudition, makes it easy to mistake Flaubert for a tedious collector of research.
difficultyReason: The sentences are clear and the events easy to follow, but because the author never states a judgment, readers must work out for themselves where a character's folly ends and the narrator's own view begins.

name: Leo Tolstoy
importanceReason: By holding hundreds of characters within a single narrative while narrating each one's consciousness from the inside, he made the individual's inner life and the scale of history coexist within one novel. He recorded death, marriage, and battle not as ideas but as a continuous sequence of sensations, setting the standard that later fiction would come to call interior description. His late theory of art and religious conversion opened up in advance the 20th century's question of whether literature can bear social responsibility, and connects directly to the lineage of nonviolent thought that includes Gandhi.
readingEntryReason: A single novella of just over 100 pages contains the whole of Tolstoy's method, letting a reader confirm what his narration does before taking on the length of a novel.
readingWarning: Starting with War and Peace makes it easy to give up partway through, because of the sheer number of characters and the essays on the philosophy of history inserted along the way. Moving from the novella to the novels in order is recommended.
difficultyReason: The sentences and psychological description are transparent and present no obstacle to reading; the real difficulty lies in the sheer length, the confusion of Russian naming conventions, and the essayistic chapters set into the middle of the novels.

name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
importanceReason: He introduced into the novel a narrative structure that lets every character push their own logic to its limit without the author rendering judgment. This structure, which Bakhtin later named polyphony, made possible a novel in which ideological argument itself becomes narrative. His first-person narrators of excessive self-consciousness, who betray even their own self-interest, became a prototype repeated by 20th-century existentialist fiction and absurdist literature, and his way of treating murder, suicide, and lost faith as experiments in ideas established the novel of ideas as a genre in its own right.
readingEntryReason: Because the skeleton of a detective story — a murder and its pursuit — carries the reading forward, it is the one novel a reader can finish to the end without already being at home in its ideological debates.
readingWarning: Starting with The Brothers Karamazov or Demons makes it easy to give up before the story even begins, because of the characters' triple Russian names and the density of ideological argument packed into the first 100 pages.
difficultyReason: The sentences themselves read quickly, but the long arguments the characters pour out repeatedly stop the narrative, and many passages assume background knowledge of 19th-century Russian religious and political debate.

name: Anton Chekhov
importanceReason: He stripped resolution and moral lesson out of narrative, and made the condition itself — characters unable to explain their own lives, dialogue that talks past itself — into the form of the work. In his short stories he established a structure that ends not in a plot twist but in a minute shift of perception, setting the basic model for the 20th-century short story. In his plays he placed the weight on what goes unsaid rather than on action on stage, laying the premises for post-Stanislavski acting technique and 20th-century realist theater.
readingEntryReason: A single story of just over 20 pages contains the whole of Chekhov's method — narration without explanation and an ending that resolves nothing — making it the surest point of entry.
readingWarning: Reading in order from the hundreds of short sketches he placed in humor magazines early on obscures what he actually changed. It is better to start with the works after 1888.
difficultyReason: The sentences are short and the vocabulary plain, but because nothing is explained, the story reads as though nothing happens unless the reader fills in what has been left out.

name: Henrik Ibsen
importanceReason: Using nothing but prose dialogue in a drawing room, he made plays that interrogate social institutions and personal lies, and established the retrospective plot — in which a hidden past collapses the present — as the basic structure of modern drama. The final exit in A Doll's House ended the convention by which European theater supplied moral reconciliation at the close. Joyce learned Norwegian just to read his plays in the original — a measure of how, to writers of the early 20th century, Ibsen was not a master of the past but a contemporary in form.
readingEntryReason: A short play that compresses three days of events into three acts, its final scene alone shows exactly what modern drama put an end to.
readingWarning: Starting with Peer Gynt only blurs what Ibsen's modern drama is, because of the sprawling structure of a verse folk-play. It is better to read the prose realist plays first.
difficultyReason: Being plays, they are short and the dialogue is clear, but a character's real motive is hidden beneath the lines, so skimming only the stage directions misses the weight of what happens.

name: Henry James
importanceReason: He moved the seat of narration from an omniscient narrator to a single character's central consciousness, and formalized point-of-view control — presenting events only to the extent that consciousness perceives them — as a technique of fiction. In the prefaces to the New York Edition he laid out a theory of point of view, construction, and dramatization, supplying vocabulary that 20th-century fiction theory and creative-writing instruction still use today. The late-style sentences that defer and withhold judgment mark the last stage before the emergence of stream-of-consciousness narration, and it was also his doing that the cultural collision of Americans in Europe became a permanent subject of the novel.
readingEntryReason: An early novella under 100 pages, it lets a reader confirm his themes and handling of point of view before encountering the difficult prose of his late style.
readingWarning: Starting with a late novel such as The Ambassadors or The Golden Bowl is almost certain to fail, because of the late style in which a single sentence can run past half a page and the key word keeps being deferred.
difficultyReason: The early works are plain, but in the late trilogy subordinate clauses pile up layer on layer and events are conveyed only through a character's conjecture, so that what actually happened is not settled unless one rereads sentence by sentence.

name: Joseph Conrad
importanceReason: He made standard devices of the novel out of frame narration, in which a narrator relays events without knowing them completely, and delayed decoding, in which the reader learns what actually happened only after the fact. In Nostromo, his method of scattering chronology to narrate the history of a nation and its capital as fractured time became something 20th-century fiction after Faulkner would use again and again. Heart of Darkness, which narrates an imperial enterprise from within while exposing the emptiness of its language, became both the target and the starting point of the postcolonial literature that writes back against it, and it is also an instance of English prose newly tuned by a Polish-born writer working in his third language.
readingEntryReason: Within novella length, both of Conrad's devices — frame narration and delayed decoding — are at work, and a reader can follow along with the debate 20th-century literature has waged with this work.
readingWarning: Starting with Nostromo, the scrambled chronology and shifting narrators mean that even who is doing what fails to come into focus for the first 200 pages.
difficultyReason: On top of dense sentences layered with adjectives, events arrive out of chronological order and filtered through multiple narrators, so the reader must reconstruct the timeline alone.

name: Machado de Assis
importanceReason: In The Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas, where an already-dead narrator hails the reader and scatters his own life across short chapters, he turned narrative reliability itself into a joke in 1881, at the height of realism. Dom Casmurro takes the structure of never ruling on whether the wife was unfaithful, leaving the verdict to the reader, and thereby set up the unreliable narrator as a design principle of the novel. These devices, which emerged from Rio de Janeiro on the empire's periphery decades ahead of European modernism, entered the canon of world literature only in the late 20th century, and with them came a fresh look at how he — the grandson of a freed slave — treated the hypocrisy of a slaveholding society.
readingEntryReason: Each chapter runs only a page or two, making it easy to enter, and because the dead narrator addresses the reader from the first chapter, his method is apparent immediately.
readingWarning: Reading from his Romantic-period works before 1872 leads to mistaking him for an ordinary regional writer. One should start with the novels from 1881 onward.
difficultyReason: Thanks to the short chapters and conversational narration, the sentences read easily, but taking the narrator's statements at face value means missing half the work, so a skeptical way of reading is required.

name: Charles Baudelaire
importanceReason: Without abandoning the rules of formal verse, he made urban ugliness, boredom, and the crowd legitimate subjects for poetry, and in Paris Spleen he established the prose poem, free of meter, as a genre in its own right. His method of evoking the idea behind an object through a correspondence of sensations, rather than explaining it, passed through Mallarmé and Rimbaud to become Symbolism, and it remained the common grammar of 20th-century poetry. The concept of modernity he set out in The Painter of Modern Life — the attitude of extracting the eternal from the transient — was permission for art to treat the surface of its own age as a legitimate subject.
readingEntryReason: As 50 short poems written in prose, it loses the least in translation, and since each piece runs two or three pages, one can start anywhere without regard to order.
readingWarning: Trying to read The Flowers of Evil straight through from the start easily feels monotonous across the whole collection, because once the formal verse's meter disappears in translation, only the allegory remains.
difficultyReason: The vocabulary itself is not difficult, but because the allegory refers to concrete objects and events of 19th-century Paris, reading without annotation means missing what many passages point to.

name: Walt Whitman
importanceReason: He established in English a free verse that breaks the line by the length of a breath instead of by rhyme and fixed meter, and made a single poem's scale large enough to hold an entire nation through nothing but the repetition of lists. By not excluding labor, the body, sex, and everyday objects from poetic diction, he removed the class restrictions that had constrained poetry's vocabulary. His practice of expanding and rearranging the same book from the first edition of 1855 until his death left behind the idea of a text that is not a finished work but one that keeps growing over a lifetime, and most of 20th-century American poetry has fixed its own position by either inheriting from him or reacting against him.
readingEntryReason: The 1855 first edition, twelve poems across 95 pages, is far shorter than the later editions, yet his inventions of free verse and the list are already fully formed in it.
readingWarning: Starting with the bulk of the 1891–92 deathbed edition tires the reader with repetition and lists first, because of an arrangement that mixes forty years of additions. The first edition, or a selection based on it, is recommended.
difficultyReason: The sentences and vocabulary are plain, but the list form strings together long runs of identically structured lines, so following it with the eye alone, as one would read prose, kills the rhythm and makes it tedious.

name: Emily Dickinson
importanceReason: Working within the short meters of the hymnal, cutting sentences with dashes and omitting grammatical connectives, she created a form that packs a sudden turn of perception into a poem of barely ten lines. By rendering death, consciousness, and the collapse of faith not in abstractions but through household objects and bodily sensation, she perfected in advance the technique of compression that 20th-century poetry would use. She published only about a dozen poems anonymously in her lifetime and left behind more than 1,700 poems bound by hand into thread-sewn manuscript booklets, making her an exceptional case of a canon formed entirely outside the publishing system.
readingEntryReason: This is the form in which her poems first reached the world, and its 115 poems form a complete single volume that lets a reader see the whole terrain. That said, Korean translations are usually based on 20th-century scholarly editions, so choosing one of those is the better option.
readingWarning: Reading a translation that simply carries over the 1890s first-edition line risks mistaking the punctuation and titles the editors imposed for the original text. Choose a translation based on a scholarly edition that preserves her dashes and capitalization.
difficultyReason: Each poem is short, but dashes and omission strip out the grammatical connections, and pronouns are left without a stated antecedent, so the reader must reconstruct the logic between lines every time.

name: Friedrich Nietzsche
importanceReason: He rewrote philosophical argument into aphorism and poetic prose, leaving behind a model of prose that thinks through style rather than system. Thus Spoke Zarathustra, a hybrid form of epic prose borrowing the style of scripture, opened a path by which a work of philosophy could be read as literature. His genealogical method of describing morality and truth not as given facts but as historically made things became, for 20th-century writers, a tool for changing the very object of narration, and he stands at the point of origin for everything from writers such as Thomas Mann and Eugene O'Neill, who openly named him as their premise, to existentialism and the literature of the absurd.
readingEntryReason: Its three essays connect to carry out a single argument to the end, so a reader can confirm what he is claiming without having to fill in the gaps between aphorisms.
readingWarning: Starting with Thus Spoke Zarathustra is the most common path, but because its fables and allusions presuppose the arguments of his earlier works, the sentences read easily while no clear claim stays with the reader.
difficultyReason: Each individual aphorism is short and its sentences ornate, so it reads easily, but the argument of a whole book lies in how the aphorisms are arranged, so that understanding at the sentence level and understanding at the book level pull apart. Another obstacle is that a posthumous compilation edited by his sister has circulated for years as though it were one of his own works.
